subject: mathematics
question_text: Prove that cos A cos(π/3 + A) cos(π/3 − A) = (1/4) cos 3A.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 8 TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS, Very Short Answer question 39(ii), book p.92. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The two marks sit on the difference-of-squares step and on recognising cos 3A; grouping the last two factors stays on the page as unmarked working. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1-Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory, and Trigonometric Ratios and Transformations holds two of those ten slots. NUMERIC CHECK before authoring: both sides were evaluated at A = 0.3, 0.7, 1.1 and 37°; they agreed to 12 decimal places at every value. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — name each move in order.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Group the last two factors
steps.margin_note: Write cos A outside a bracket and keep the matched pair inside it. Note the formula mixes cos² with sin², unlike the sine version.
lines: L.H.S = cos A · [cos(π/3 + A) cos(π/3 − A)]
cos(X + Y) cos(X − Y) = cos²X − sin²Y

recall.must_convey: That the last two factors are grouped as a sum times a difference, ready for cos²X − sin²Y.
accept: keep cos a outside and bracket the other two
cos x plus y into cos x minus y is cos squared x minus sin squared y
the second and third factors are a matched pair
rendu factors ni bracket lo pettali

steps.why: The second and third factors are a sum and a difference of the same two angles, so they multiply to a difference of squares. cos A is left outside for now.
common_mistakes: Expanding cos(π/3 + A) and cos(π/3 − A) term by term.
Writing the result as cos²X − cos²Y.
steps.memory_tip: For cosines the pair gives cos²X − sin²Y — a cosine square minus a sine square.

steps.label: Apply cos(X+Y) cos(X−Y)
steps.margin_note: First mark. The bracket first becomes 1/4 − sin²A; replacing sin²A by 1 − cos²A turns it into cos²A − 3/4.
lines: With X = π/3 and Y = A:

recall.must_convey: That the bracket becomes cos²(π/3) − sin²A = 1/4 − sin²A, and then cos²A − 3/4.
accept: x is pi by three and y is a so it is cos squared pi by three minus sin squared a
cos pi by three squared is one by four
replace sin squared a by one minus cos squared a to get cos squared a minus three by four
sin square ni one minus cos square ga marchali
apply the difference of squares formula
reject: cos three a is four cos cubed a minus three cos a

steps.why: cos(π/3) = 1/2, so its square is 1/4. Changing sin²A to 1 − cos²A is needed because cos 3A is written in cosines only.
common_mistakes: Leaving sin²A in place, which cannot give cos 3A.

steps.label: Recognise cos 3A
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Multiply cos A in, then take 1/4 out of both terms. What is left is the standard expansion of cos 3A.

recall.must_convey: That cos A (cos²A − 3/4) = (1/4)(4 cos³A − 3 cos A) = (1/4) cos 3A.
accept: multiply cos a in and take one by four out
four cos cubed a minus three cos a is cos three a
so the left side is a quarter of cos three a
one by four bayaki teeste cos three a vasthundi
the answer is one by four cos three a
reject: apply the difference of squares formula

steps.why: Multiplying cos A into the bracket gives cos³A − (3/4)cos A. Taking 1/4 out leaves 4 cos³A − 3 cos A, which is exactly cos 3A.
common_mistakes: Taking 1/4 out of only one term.
Writing cos 3A as 3 cos A − 4 cos³A, which is the sine pattern.
steps.memory_tip: cos 3A = 4 cos³A − 3 cos A: cosine starts with 4, sine starts with 3.
